---
title: "Errors using LMMs when one or more predictors correlate with the group or unit effects"
format: html
---

We're fitting linear mixed effects models to quantify variation in some outcome, e.g. trait, with respect to environment within and across species. However, we found that a standard linear mixed effects model gives a biased result. In particular, when traits have a flat response within species, but positive across species, a linear mixed effects model will suggest that the within  species traits are also positive. 

This bias arises because of an effect described in the reference below. 
- Based on Bafumi, J., & Gelman, A. (2011). Fitting Multilevel Models When Predictors and Group Effects Correlate. SSRN Electronic Journal. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.1010095

This document attempts to illustrate the bias using simulated data. 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(easystats)
library(glmmTMB)
library(patchwork)

```

# Generate data

We're going to generate two datasets. 

- `data1`: satisifies assumptions of a standard random effects model setup. In particular groups do not differ in their average x values, `x_mn`
- `data2`: does not satisify assumptions of a standard random effects model setup, as groups differ in their average x values `x_mn` and group intercepts are correlated with `x_mn`. 

## Data1
```{r}
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Simulate data
n_species <- 8 # Number of species
n_obs <- 80 # Number of obs

# Create a dataset
data1 <- tibble(
  species_id = rep(1:n_species, each = n_obs / n_species), # 10 species
  x = runif(n_obs, 1, 10), # X variable
  x_mn = 5.5,
  x_c = x - x_mn
)

# Assign random intercepts and slopes per group
random_intercepts1 <- rnorm(n_species, mean = 50, sd = 10) # Varying intercepts
random_slopes1 <- rnorm(n_species, mean = 3, sd = 3) # Varying slopes

# Generate test y based on random effects
data1 <- data |>
  mutate(
    species = letters[species_id], # Convert species to a factor
    intercept = random_intercepts1[species_id],
    slope = random_slopes1[species_id],
    y_mn = intercept + slope * x,
    y = y_mn + rnorm(n_obs, 0, 3) # Adding noise
  )


plot_1_true <-
  ggplot(data1, aes(x = x, y = y, color = species, group = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_mn), size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "True relationships") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

plot_1_true
```

## Data2

```{r}
set.seed(125)
# Simulate data
n_species <- 8 # Number of species
n_obs <- 80 # Number of obs

# Create a dataset
data2 <- tibble(
  species_id = rep(1:n_species, each = n_obs / n_species), # 10 species
  x_c = runif(n_obs, -6, 6) # X variable
)

# Generate random x_mn for groups
x_mn <- rnorm(n_species, mean = 50, sd = 20) |> sort()
random_intercepts2 <- rnorm(n_species, mean = 5, sd = 1.5)

# Generate on average flatter than main fixed effect
random_slopes2 <- rnorm(n_species, mean = 0.05, sd = 0.1) # Varying slopes

fixed_effect_slope <- 0.3

# Generate test y based on random effects
data2 <- data2 |>
  mutate(
    species = letters[species_id], # Convert species to a factor
    intercept = random_intercepts2[species_id],
    slope = random_slopes2[species_id],
    x_mn = x_mn[species_id],
    x = x_mn + x_c,
    y_mn = intercept + x_mn * fixed_effect_slope + slope * x_c,
    y = y_mn + rnorm(n_obs, 0, 1.5) # Adding noise
  )

plot_2_true <-
  ggplot(data2, aes(x = x, y = y, color = species, group = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_mn), size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "True relationships") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

plot_2_true
```

# LMM works for data1

This section demonstrates that a linear mixed effects model works well for data1, where the assumptions are satisfied. We fit three models, a null model with just fixed effect, a random intercept model, and a random intercept and slope model. We expect the final model to do best, as that reflects the underlying generating process. 

```{r}
# Simple model
model_0 <- glmmTMB(y ~ x, data = data1)

# Random intercept model
model_intercept <- glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | species), data = data1)

# Random intercept & slope model
model_intercept_slope <- glmmTMB(y ~ x + (x | species), data = data1)

parameters(model_intercept_slope)
```

The parameters of the fitted model suggests it does a reasonable job at recovering estimates of true parameters. 
- intercept: true mean equals 50, sd = 20
- slope: true value mean = 3, sd = 3

We can also make some plots to highlight that the Random slopes and intercepts model is much closer to the true relationships. Also indicated is the average error being the difference between the group level slopes and their true values. 

```{r}
# No random effects
means_all <- estimate_expectation(model_0, by = "x")

p0 <-
  ggplot(data1, aes(x = x, y = y, color = species, group = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = means_all, aes(y = Predicted, group = ""), col = "black", size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Standard model:\n\t\t y ~ x") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Random intercept model
means_j <- estimate_expectation(model_intercept)
means_all <- estimate_expectation(model_intercept, by = "x")

p1 <-
  ggplot(data1, aes(x = x, y = y, color = species, group = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = means_j, aes(y = Predicted), size = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = means_all, aes(y = Predicted, group = ""), col = "black", size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Random Intercepts:\n\t\t y ~ x + (1 | species)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Random slope and intercepts
means_j <- estimate_expectation(model_intercept_slope)
means_all <- estimate_expectation(model_intercept_slope, by = "x")

p3 <-
  ggplot(data1, aes(x = x, y = y, color = species, group = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = means_j, aes(y = Predicted), size = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = means_all, aes(y = Predicted, group = ""), col = "black", size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Random slope & intercepts:\n\t\t y ~ x + (x | species)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Combine plots
p_fits_1 <- plot_1_true + p0 + p1 + p3

p_fits_1
# ggsave("outputs/mixed_effects_models.png", p_all, width = 12, height = 5)

``` 

# Modified LMM is better works for data2

Now we show that with data2, the modified LMM fits MUCH better than a standard LMM. In both cases, we fit random slopes and intercepts model, reflecting the data generation process. 

In this dataset the true values of parameters are

- overall slope = 0.3
- within species slope: mean 0.05, sd = 0.1
- overall intercept: mean = 5,
- within species intercept: mean = 0,  sd = 1.5

```{r}
# Standard LMM with random intercept & slope model
model_intercept_slope1 <- glmmTMB(y ~ x + (x | species), data = data2)
# Modified LMM with random intercept & slope model
model_intercept_slope2 <- glmmTMB(y ~ x_mn + x_c + (x_c | species), data = data2)

parameters(model_intercept_slope1)
parameters(model_intercept_slope2)
```

The standard model fails on multiple fronts 

- there were convergence errors fitting the standard LMM
- attributes the variation between groups to the intercept rather than the slope.  
- CI for fitted parameters does not contain the true values, whereas the modified model does.


And to illustrate with some plots: 

```{r}
p2 <- 
  ggplot(data2, aes(x = x, y = y, color = species, group = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = y_mn), size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "True relationships") +
  ylim(c(10, 30)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Random slope and intercepts
means_j1 <- estimate_expectation(model_intercept_slope1)

p3 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x = x, y = y, color = species, group = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = means_j1, aes(y = Predicted), size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Classic mixed model:\n\t\t y ~ x + (x | species)") +
  ylim(c(10, 30)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Random slope and intercepts
means_j2 <- estimate_expectation(model_intercept_slope2) |>
  mutate(x = x_mn + x_c)

p4 <-
  ggplot(data2, aes(x = x, y = y, color = species, group = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = means_j2, aes(y = Predicted), size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Modified mixed model:\n\t\t y ~ x_mn + x_c + (x_c | species)") +
  theme_classic() +
  ylim(c(10, 30)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Combine plots
p_mm <- p2 + p3 + p4
p_mm
# ggsave("outputs/mixed_effects_models2.png", p_mm, width = 12, height = 5)

``` 

# Modified LMM with random intercept & slope model using brms

```{r}
library(brms)

model_intercept_slope2_brms <- brm(
  y ~ x_mn + x_c + (x_c | species),
  data = data2,
  family = gaussian(),
  chains = 3,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 3
)

summary(model_intercept_slope2_brms)
parameters(model_intercept_slope2)
```

# Example fitting with custom stan model via rstan

```{r}
library(rstan)

# Prepare data for Stan
stan_data <- list(
  N = nrow(data2),
  J = length(unique(data2$species)),
  species = as.integer(as.factor(data2$species)),
  x_mn = data2$x_mn,
  x_c = data2$x_c,
  y = data2$y
)

# Define Stan model
stan_model_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> N;              // number of observations
  int<lower=0> J;              // number of species
  array[N] int<lower=1,upper=J> species;  // species indicator
  vector[N] x_mn;              // group mean predictor
  vector[N] x_c;               // centered predictor
  vector[N] y;                 // response variable
}
parameters {
  real beta_0;                 // intercept
  real beta_mn;                // coefficient for x_mn
  real beta_c;                 // coefficient for x_c
  vector[J] u_0;               // random intercepts
  vector[J] u_c;               // random slopes
  real<lower=0> sigma_u0;      // sd of random intercepts
  real<lower=0> sigma_uc;      // sd of random slopes
  real<lower=0> sigma;         // residual sd
}
model {
  vector[N] mu;

  // Priors
  beta_0 ~ normal(0, 10);
  beta_mn ~ normal(0, 10);
  beta_c ~ normal(0, 10);
  sigma_u0 ~ cauchy(0, 5);
  sigma_uc ~ cauchy(0, 5);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
  u_0 ~ normal(0, sigma_u0);
  u_c ~ normal(0, sigma_uc);

  // Likelihood
  for (i in 1:N) {
    mu[i] = beta_0 + u_0[species[i]] + beta_mn * x_mn[i] + (beta_c + u_c[species[i]]) * x_c[i];
  }
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}
"

# Fit model
model_intercept_slope2_stan <- stan(
  model_code = stan_model_code,
  data = stan_data,
  chains = 3,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  cores = 3
)

print(model_intercept_slope2_stan, pars = c("beta_0", "beta_mn", "beta_c", "sigma_u0", "sigma_uc", "sigma"))
summary(model_intercept_slope2_brms)
parameters(model_intercept_slope2)
```
